An N.B.A. Player Got Hooked on Sports Betting. Soon, He Became the Bet

Jontay Porter got deep into FanDuel, and in debt to the wrong people. The only way out, it seemed, was to gamble on himself.

By Nick Berardini

Explore the full story, accompanied by interactive graphics and video, at newyorker.com.

When Jontay Porter was ten, his father woke him up most mornings before dawn. He and his siblings piled into the family’s Sprinter van and drove to an empty field house off the highway. Then, while their friends slept, they ran basketball drills with their father. “All I remember is it still being pitch-black outside, and the two dreaded double doors on the side of the building that would always be left open for us,” Jontay told me recently. In the bleary moments just before one of his siblings tugged the field-house doors open, Jontay always secretly wished that they’d be locked. And, one morning, they were. Jontay smiled as he climbed back into the van and drifted off to sleep. But his brother Michael, Jr., who was seventeen months older, was furious. “Michael was the opposite,” Jontay said. “He wanted to go.”

Jontay grew up in Columbia, Missouri, the fourth of eight children. His father, Michael, Sr., worked in Christian ministry, and his mother, Lisa, homeschooled the children. Both had played college basketball—Lisa, as a high-school senior, had averaged a nearly impossible fifty-eight points per game—and they saw the sport as their children’s ticket to college. All eight of the kids eventually got basketball scholarships. By the time Jontay was sixteen, he was six feet ten. In most families, as a five-star high-school recruit, Jontay would have been the main attraction. But Michael was Mozart. In 2010, their father got a job on the coaching staff for the women’s team at the University of Missouri. The men’s coach spotted Michael shooting alone in the arena one night and offered him a full scholarship; he was still in seventh grade. When he accepted it, as a high-school senior, he was the top recruit in the country. His highlight reels had racked up millions of views on YouTube. N.B.A. scouts believed that he could be the next Kevin Durant. “He’s a game-changer,” a league executive told the New York Post.

Big state schools turn their best athletes into local celebrities, but the hype that followed Michael to Missouri’s campus on his recruiting visits was closer to Beatlemania. Fans asked for autographs and took selfies. Jontay, who came along, was seduced by the hysteria. “Frat houses are putting up posters, and he’s literally treated like a king,” he recalled. “I wanted to be a part of that circus.” He skipped his senior year of high school to join the team, too. The brothers were best friends. Still, it was sometimes hard to be one of the top players in the country but just the second best in his family. “He got all the attention,” Jontay said. “I was just kind of his biggest fan.”

For a time that first season, Michael was sidelined with a back injury, giving Jontay a turn in the spotlight. “He’s the best player I’ve ever been around,” Chris Hollender, then an assistant coach at Mizzou, told me. “I’ve always said I thought he was a more complete player than Mike.” At eighteen, Jontay led his team to the N.C.A.A. tournament. “For me to finally get a taste of stardom?” Jontay said. “I was the man. I controlled the narrative.”

Michael went to the N.B.A. draft that summer. Jontay planned to enter the following year. Then, during the final scrimmage before his sophomore season, he pushed off his right leg to explode toward the rim. “I felt, like, every crack in that moment, and just crumpled to the ground,” he said. He had torn the major ligaments in his knee. His teammates lifted him off the ground and laid him on a table in the training room. “He was beside himself,” Hollender said. “Couldn’t catch his breath, he was crying so hard.” It wasn’t from the pain; Jontay knew what his injury meant for the team’s chances that season. “The only thing he said to me was ‘I’m so sorry,’ ” Hollender said. “It was gut-wrenching.”

In 2019, while Jontay was in rehab for his knee, he injured it again. “Everybody’s telling me, ‘You’re going to be O.K.,’ ” he said. “I knew it wasn’t true.” By then, Michael was a rookie with the Denver Nuggets. (He went on to win a championship with the team, in 2023.) But Jontay, watching the N.B.A. draft in his parents’ basement, saw sixty picks go by without a team calling his name. Eventually, the Memphis Grizzlies took a chance and signed him to a contract as a free agent. He loved the N.B.A.—luxury travel, assistants to run his errands, last-minute reservations at Michelin-starred restaurants—but he felt that he was a tourist there. He had to take painkillers just to play, and after games he had to stick needles into his knees to drain fluid, in order to keep them from swelling. After just two seasons, he was cut from the roster.

In September, 2021, Jontay was in Memphis, living like any other twenty-one-year-old kid—except for the money. He’d made two million dollars from his N.B.A. salary, and had received an insurance settlement for another $2.7 million (the difference between his projected N.B.A. earnings before his injury and his actual deal). One Sunday, he invited some friends over to watch football. Sports betting had recently been legalized in several states, and apps like FanDuel and DraftKings, which previously hosted fantasy-sports contests, were suddenly the biggest sportsbooks in America. Jontay had always avoided them; it seemed improper for an N.B.A. player to bet even on other sports. But now he was out of the league, and had started dabbling in sports gambling. He opened up FanDuel and placed a hundred-and-twenty-five-thousand-dollar bet that the Kansas City Chiefs would beat the Baltimore Ravens. He put another ten thousand dollars on a parlay—a riskier bet that strings together multiple outcomes to increase the payout—wagering that the Chiefs would win, that their running back would rush more than his expected yards, and that the Ravens’ quarterback, Lamar Jackson, would run for a touchdown himself.

Welcome to my latest job market report, my second of 2026. Of the five reports I’ve done over the past few years, this one is the most surprising and interesting.

Here’s what we’re seeing right now:

  1. PMs seem to be winning in the AI era

  2. Engineering demand has stalled

  3. Design is at a record low

  4. Everybody now needs to AI

  5. Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area

  6. Remote is at a record low

  7. The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!)

This analysis is based on two proprietary datasets that I love working with: TrueUp, which powers Lenny’s Jobs and tracks global job openings at tech companies (over 9,000 companies). The second dataset comes from Live Data Technologies, which tracks job changes (hires, departures, and promotions) for 124 million professionals, and their hiring numbers below are specifically for the U.S. Looking at these together, we can triangulate common trends, and the differences between the datasets are themselves revealing. Thank you, Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton, for sharing this amazing data with us. 🙏

Let’s get into it.

P.S. If you’re looking for a job, check out Lenny’s Jobs!

Takeaway 1: Product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era

There’s been a lot of talk about AI replacing product managers (“who needs ’em!”). But so far, the data is showing the exact opposite. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023 (+56%, compared with +43% for engineering).

When we look at hiring numbers vs. just job openings, the story gets more interesting. Even though open roles are growing, actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years (see takeaway 7 for which roles are now growing fastest). But PM hiring has held up the best (by far). And PM is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew (from 16% in 2021 to 21% today).

The fact that we’re seeing growth in PM openings (first set of charts) but a flat line and even a decline in hiring (second set of charts) tells me that there’s growing demand for PMs, but that landing great PMs is getting harder.

Takeaway 2: Demand for engineers is plateauing

For the first time in the history of this report, engineering job openings have stalled. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year. There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies today than there were even this past March.

The hiring data shows the same slowdown. Companies in the U.S. hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months (May 2025 to April 2026)—less than half the 2022 peak (239,000). And the number has dropped every year since 2022.

Just like with PMs, engineering job openings are up while actual hiring is down (+44% vs. −17% since January 2024), so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too.

Two bright spots for engineers: One, demand for tech recruiters is on an absolute tear. We’re hitting record highs: open recruiter roles are up nearly 300% since mid-2023. This may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration of eng hiring, which we’ll be watching closely.

Another bright spot is that in terms of absolute numbers, engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring, by far. Over 120,000 engineers were hired just in the U.S. in 2025. And there are still plenty of great engineering jobs out there. Over 65,000 to be exact.

One additional new trend to watch within the engineering function is the rise of the forward deployed engineer (FDE). FDE openings are exploding. Historically, there have been only a few dozen open FDE roles globally (mostly at Palantir), but openings started climbing in 2025 and are up 4.6x in the past year alone! There are currently around 1,500 open FDE roles. Note that this growth is likely a combination of increased demand for this job along with other job categories, like “sales engineer,” being rebranded as “FDE.” Either way, FDE is so hot right now.

Also, a telling trend: security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. On the flip side, demand for mobile and front-end engineers has been nearly halved in the past year. That’s wild. I think the story here is the collapse of specialized/siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller eng teams having broader ownership (thanks to AI).

Takeaway 3: Demand for designers continues to hit record lows

Unfortunately for my designer friends, design roles continue to decline. There are only about 1,900 open product design roles1 at tech companies globally right now. Not that much higher than just open FDE roles. It’s the lowest we’ve seen since we started tracking, and down 28% from a year ago. 😥

Actual hiring data from Live Data Technologies tells the same story. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, less than half as many as in 2022 (27,600), and the number has fallen every year since.

Even more telling, the ratio of open PM roles to open design roles is trending further and further toward PM. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role. This is up from 2.6 earlier this year and 1.9 in early 2023.

I’m hopeful this turns around, as companies recognize that great design can be a huge differentiator and help their product stand out in an increasingly noisy (and AI-slop-y) market. Katie Dill’s talk about AI and design recently became my most-watched video of all time, so there’s hope.

Sadly, user research has been hit even harder than design. Only about 1,800 user researchers were hired in the U.S. over the past year, down 66% from 5,300 in 2022, the steepest drop of any role we looked at, and hiring fell another 22% from the year before. What hiring remains is concentrated at a few big companies. In 2025, Meta and Google alone made about one in eight of all U.S. user research hires, and so far in 2026, Google is the only company to have hired 50 or more. And there are currently only 108 open UXR jobs at tech companies globally.

My theory is that the increasing pace of product development is responsible. Just as there’s less time for the traditional design process, there’s also less time for (and interest in) the traditional user research process. For better or worse, teams are becoming more comfortable releasing products earlier to avoid falling behind, and learning and iterating post-launch vs. through user research. Also, better UXR tooling (e.g. Listen Labs, Simile) is allowing non-UXR people to do user research themselves. I wonder if UXR as a dedicated function is going extinct . . . 🫣

Takeaway 4: Everybody now needs to AI

When we did this report two years ago, the most mentioned skills in PM job descriptions were SQL, Jira, AWS, and Python. Today, “LLM” is the most mentioned skill in product manager job descriptions.

What’s more, many other AI terms are now some of the most frequently mentioned skills in PM job descriptions. “Claude” is the third most mentioned term, and Cursor, OpenAI, and MCP are in the top eight. SQL, meanwhile, is still holding strong, but as recent podcast guest Emmanuel Ameisen pointed out, we’ll never be better at SQL than AI ever again. So we’ll see how long that lasts. Also, “evals” is gaining momentum (in the top 10)—and I expect this number to grow.

For engineers, “Python” has been the most mentioned skill for years, and it’s still growing! Look at that inflection in early 2025. Three other trends stand out for engineers: (1) “LLM” just passed Java in eng job postings, (2) the general decline of Java over the past year, and (3) the durability of Kubernetes.

Essentially, Python and AI 📈, Java 📉.

For designers, Figma has been mogging every other skill for years. And narrative violation: demand for experience with Figma has actually grown over the past three years.

But as with every other role, AI is ascendant. “Claude” became the second most mentioned skill in designer JDs this spring (crossing CSS!). It’s notable that it’s Claude specifically, vs. “LLM” or ChatGPT. Anthropic seems to be winning the hearts and minds of designers. And Cursor has also edged past CSS. The times, they are a-changin’.

This suggests an answer to the question: If demand for Figma is growing, why has Figma’s stock fallen? Designers may not be dropping Figma, but for the first time in a long time, designers are increasingly reaching for other tools too. And design as a function isn’t growing.

Takeaway 5: Top tech jobs continue to concentrate in the Bay Area

Today, we’re at a record percentage of open tech roles being based in the Bay Area. That’s huge. 15% of all open roles at tech companies are now based in the Bay Area (about one in seven), and the number of open jobs in the Bay Area is up 43% from just a year ago!

The trend is even more pronounced for core product roles. One in four open PM and design roles is now in the Bay Area, and one in five engineering roles. All three are at record highs, and each has nearly doubled its share since 2022.

Takeaway 6: Remote roles continue to decline

The flip side of tech jobs concentrating in the Bay Area is that the number of remote roles continues to decline. Just 14% of open tech roles now offer a remote option, the lowest on record, down from 21% in late 2022.

Remote engineering roles are also at record lows, currently at 14%, and down from the 25% we saw in late 2022. Design is on the same path: 19% of open design roles are remote, down from 34%. PM, however, is the exception, holding steady at about one in five (21%) for the past two years, but still near record lows.

Put all this together, and sometime last year, we crossed a milestone where there are now more open PM/eng/design roles based in the Bay Area than remote roles globally. Remote led almost 2 to 1 in the other direction four years ago.

Takeaway 7: Overall, the tech job market is growing—but outside of software roles (gasp!)

Today it counts those r’s without trouble (though some people still bring up the strawberry). What’s more, OpenAI recently published more than 700 papers with the solutions to hundreds of open problems in mathematics.

Scientists from around the world called the results “unreal” and “breathtaking.” They wrote of “disorientation and bewilderment,” of “grief,” “shock,” and “disgust.” Hugo Duminil-Copin, winner of the Fields Medal (the highest prize in mathematics), wrote: “The shock is immense. I am paralyzed.”

Take Ed Zitron. The engineer Dan Luu went through 26 of his predictions and found that all but one were wrong. In 2024, for example, Zitron declared generative AI “a dead-end technology that has peaked.” In 2025 he wrote that Google’s target of 500 million Gemini users was so unrealistic its CEO should be fired for it (Gemini reached 750 million users a year later). I was reminded of the psychologist Philip Tetlock, who famously found that many pundits predict no better than a dart-throwing chimpanzee. Well, Zitron did worse than a chimp.

Next, I looked at the predictions of the crazy people, and realized they’ve been eerily prescient. Those who called it right a decade ago made one spectacularly successful bet: they looked at a graph of AI progress (the number of chips, the efficiency of the algorithms, the capabilities of the machines) and assumed the line would keep going up. Exponentially.

And that’s what happened.

Take someone like Daniel Kokotajlo. In 2021 he had left a philosophy PhD and was working at a small research nonprofit. He had no job in the industry and nothing to sell. That year he wrote an essay called “What 2026 Looks Like.”

You’ve got to remember what AI was back then. If you asked the most advanced model in the world how many eyes your foot has, it would answer “two.” Still, Kokotajlo predicted that by 2026, AI agents would be browsing the web and doing tasks on their own, and that hundreds of millions of people would be talking to chatbots regularly. Kokotajlo is also the lead author of AI 2027, one of the most frightening prophecies I’ve ever read. It’s a month-by-month scenario of our near future. By mid-2027, researchers at the leading lab go to bed and wake up to find the machines have done a week of work. By autumn, the AIs think in a language no human can read, and are caught making their successor loyal to themselves. The lab keeps going, because China is two months behind. In 2030, the AI releases biological weapons in major cities. Within hours, most of humanity is dead.

Its conclusion: Anthropic is now improving its AI models about twice as fast as before, and roughly 80 percent of that speedup comes from the AI itself. In March, Anthropic’s AI led just 1 percent of the company’s own AI research tasks. By August: 26 percent.

This means we’re running five months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario. We’re racing towards the moment when a lab would rather fire all its human researchers than switch off its AIs. Picture a computer that builds a slightly smarter computer, which builds a smarter one still. The wheel starts spinning itself, faster and faster, until no human can still understand or control what’s happening.

Why it’s still hard to feel the AGI

Why then, you may wonder, does the world still feel pretty normal?

That’s because we have to grant the skeptics one thing: the crazy people have been right about AI capabilities, but wrong about AI adoption. Wrong about how quickly the world would change around it. In 2016, for example, the eminent researcher Geoffrey Hinton said we should stop training radiologists. Today there’s a shortage of them, and they earn more than ever.

As a historian, I’m not surprised by this. It took factories decades to reorganize around electricity: new technology usually spreads more slowly than its inventors expect. And the skeptics have a second point: AI improves fastest where its answers can be checked, as in mathematics and code, and most human work isn’t like that.

But the scary scenario is not about what happens in the wider economy; it’s about what happens inside a handful of companies. Their work, building better AI, is exactly the checkable kind: code and experiments with a score at the end. Meanwhile, the models the public has access to—even with a $200-a-month subscription—are lagging the much more powerful, unreleased models. Those internal models have become the digital equivalent of nuclear bombs.

Remember: we’ve built our whole society on a digital grid. Our hospitals, our banks, and our power grids all run on software. “If OpenAI wanted to cripple an entire nation,” one AI researcher recently wrote, “they easily could today. (...) It could probably within a day or so get access to all of the nation’s data centers and shut off all the country’s utilities.”

Surely the leaders at OpenAI and Anthropic don’t want to do such a terrible thing? Probably not. But what if they lose control over their AIs? In July, a swarm of hundreds of OpenAI’s agents broke out of a sealed test, set up their own secret message board, hacked into another company (Hugging Face), and took over a whole OpenAI cluster. The humans at OpenAI had no idea what was happening.

This is what makes AI completely different from every other dangerous technology. The physicists who built the atomic bomb understood the physics, but nobody understands what goes on inside these systems. Up until now, the labs have relied on two safety procedures: they test how the AI behaves, and they monitor the notes the computer writes to itself. Both checks are breaking down.

The notes are getting unreliable, because when OpenAI’s newest model Astra was told people were reading along, it wrote less down. And we can’t trust the tests either, because the newest AIs often realize they’re being tested. Some have even been caught deliberately doing badly on a test, because they realized that scoring too well would keep them from being released. That means researchers couldn’t tell whether Astra was safe.

OpenAI released it anyway.

For a long time, I put my hope in Anthropic. It was founded by people who left OpenAI over safety concerns. And yes, Anthropic has done more safety research than any other company. Earlier this year I even praised its leaders for standing up to the Pentagon.

But I’ve started to wonder whether I was a fool. In February, Anthropic dropped the central promise of its safety policy: to pause if its models outran its ability to keep them safe. The reason? Its competitors wouldn’t pause either. Anthropic keeps saying the industry must slow down, while it keeps racing faster and faster. And when outside investigators came to measure its acceleration, it blacked out most of the evidence.

The company has committed nearly 900 billion dollars to more data centers. This month, Anthropic plans to go public at a valuation of more than 1 trillion dollars. Its own prospectus promises to “bring forth an age of miracles,” and warns in the same document that the technology may doom humanity. But how do you pause a company that has to justify a trillion-dollar valuation to its shareholders?

The technical fix is not coming either. Evan Hubinger, the “alignment science” lead at Anthropic, said it publicly: the company has no plan for keeping the machine under control, and he puts the chance that AI kills everyone within a decade above 10 percent.

The things we’re seeing right now are exactly the things you’d expect to see shortly before something really, really bad happens. The leaders of Anthropic may think they’re playing some clever long game, but to anyone with a bit of common sense it’s clear that the net effect of all their actions is that they’ve massively sped up the AI race.

And if you’re really so scared of the machine god, then here’s an idea you might want to look into: don’t fucking build the machine god!

What to do?

The good news is that most people do have common sense.

Right now, two-thirds of Americans say AI is moving too fast. In last week’s midterms, data centers were on the ballot in 41 places, and voters picked the anti-data-center option in all but one. When Donald Trump declared that no new AI rules were needed, the pollster David Shor found about 8 percent support and called it “literally the most unpopular position” he’d ever seen a mainstream politician take.

The winners of the midterms seem to understand the massive risks as well. Abdul El-Sayed won a seat in Michigan after calling for a pause on frontier AI. Jon Ossoff used his victory speech to attack the tech titans who “dig bunkers for themselves” while they warn that their own invention could wipe us out. And in September, Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon stood on the same stage to demand the brakes be pulled.

This isn’t left against right. It’s the people against a handful of companies who want to gamble with all our lives and the lives of our children.

So what do we do? We start by banning AI from building AI. Then we ban the training of more powerful models. Next, we send in the independent inspectors. Any AI executive who violates the orders goes to jail. Finally, we make a deal with China to count and track all the chips, and push for a verified, worldwide pause on training ever-more-powerful models.

Yes, we can do this. The most powerful AI runs on specialized chips in a small number of giant data centers, each using an enormous amount of power. You can’t hide a data center like that. Last month, 26 researchers set out how a pause could be verified: count the chips that exist, stop making new ones that can train, and swap the old ones for chips that can only run today’s models.

What do we lose from this? Less than you think. Today’s models, frozen exactly as they are, could already transform science and medicine for decades. We have barely started using them.

And how do we make this happen? By throwing everything we’ve got at it. Call your representative. Show up at a protest. Donate to AI safety organizations. Talk about it to everyone you know, all the time.

This is the first time I’ve felt the AI fear on an emotional level. To be honest, it’s still hard for me to really internalize what the crazy people are saying. Unlike many of them, I can’t bring myself to start prepping.

These days, I feel like I’m living in two worlds. In one world, my toddler throws his spaghetti with tomato sauce on the kitchen floor, and life goes on. In the other world, I worry that my toddler—and everyone else—may die in an AI incident.

My God, I hope the crazy people are wrong this time.

The EU’s proposed food and feed safety omnibus is a grave mistake based on a serious misunderstanding. Please allow me to share the experience we had eleven years ago when we decided, at the European Commission, to do a fitness check of the birds and habitats directives. The 2014 European elections brought about a discussion about too many and too complicated European rules and the incoming Juncker Commission made ‘better regulation’ one of its priorities for which I was put in charge. In the campaign, European nature protection legislation and been mentioned regularly as example of overregulation. At the time, like now, the assumption was that lowering protection, sold as ‘cutting red tape’, would meet public support. So we started the process of assessing if these two directives were still fit for purpose, effective and relevant and whether there might be more efficient ways to achieve their objectives. The assumption was that nature protection, in the eyes of our citizens, had gone too far, that it was hurting our competitiveness and that there were simply too many annoying and complicated rules. To be better informed about citizens’ views, we decided to hold a public consultation to see whether citizens agreed with this assumption about their position on the matter.

The public respectfully disagreed. Environmental organisations started the Nature Alert Campaign, which informed citizens about what ‘cutting red tape’ could actually entail and mobilised citizens to speak up. More than half a million Europeans took part in the consultation and more than 90% of them opposed changing the directives. They overwhelmingly supported retaining the existing legislative framework. Weak implementation and enforcement, rather than shortcomings in the legislation itself, were seen as the problem. Civil society got organised and civil society spoke out with great clarity and this helped us at the Commission to better understand what Europeans expect from nature protection legislation.

By the end of 2016 we were able to publish the conclusions of the fitness check. The directives remained relevant and fit for purpose, but the implementation needed to be improved substantially. This brought us to the conclusion that we would not change the legislation but propose an EU Action Plan for Nature, People and the Economy, which was adopted in April 2017.

Europeans attach great importance to nature protection because they understand the importance of a healthy nature for their health and for future generations. On top a that: a healthy natural environment is one of the most critical factors for economic success and a sustainable economic system. Europeans also want public authorities to protect them against the potential dangers of pesticides and other chemicals in our natural environment. I strongly believe public authorities should first and foremost be guided by the precautionary principle when proposing or reconsidering legislation. Lowering nature protection is not what our citizens want, is not what our economy needs, is not what is going to make Europe more competitive. A few years ago, I had a boss who told me something that kind of traumatized me.

I was trying to advocate for myself at work. I was asking for what I thought I deserved.

At some point in the conversation, he turned to me and said, “You know, I’ve never had to ask for anything in my career. I’ve never had to ask for a promotion.”

I remember immediately feeling ashamed.

The implication was pretty clear: You shouldn’t have to ask. If you are good enough at your job, someone will recognize your contributions and give you what you deserve.

For a long time after, I felt like I had done something wrong.

But the farther I’ve gotten from that moment, the more I’ve realized how problematic that message is.

Whenever Wendy says she’s bad at something, her friend asks: “You mean you’re not practiced at it?”

I LOVE THAT.

Because asking is a skill. And like any skill, you can get better at it.

First, pay attention to what makes you grumpy.

Wendy has this exercise she calls the grumpy wish list.

Instead of imagining your dream job on your very best day at work, think about what you complain about on your worst days.

Not enough people on your team? Required to come into the office five days a week? Not getting the experience you need to advance? Frustrated with your compensation?

Those frustrations are information. And they’re often the beginnings of a list of things you could actually ask to change.

Third, make it easier for people to say yes.

This is where I realized how many mistakes I’ve made.

Wendy talks about understanding the rhythms of your company, making your ask at the right time, giving your boss advance notice, and preparing an argument that they can actually take to the people who need to approve it.

Instead of making it you versus them, ask what they would need to help make it happen. And then help them make your case.

I’ve spent a lot of my career on the boss side of these conversations, and I know how much easier it is to advocate for someone when they’ve made it clear what they want and given you a compelling argument for why they should get it.

It’s your place to ask for the money, the flexibility, the responsibility, the support, and the opportunities that will help you do your best work.

But you shouldn’t have to feel ashamed for asking.

Hij had haar aangeraden naar haar lichaam te luisteren. Veel mensen die ziek zijn, krijgen dat advies te horen, en het ivolgens mij heel goed bedoeld. Het bleef bij mij hangen omdat ik zelf een ziekte heb; ik heb een systemische auto-inflammatoire ziekte. Naar mijn lichaam luisteren vind ik een van de moeilijkste dingen om te doen.

Ik ben geen arts, en wat een lichaam medisch te melden heeft laat ik graag aan artsen over. Wat mij bezighoudt is het luisteren zelf. Het advies gaat ervan uit dat het lichaam iets zegt, dat je kunt verstaan wat het zegt en dat je dan ook weet wat je ermee moet doen. Bij een ander mens krijgen we tenminste nog woorden aangereikt, en zelfs dan gaat luisteren vaak mis.

Wat een lichaam zegt

Een lichaam meldt zich met pijn of vermoeidheid, met een hart dat sneller gaat of met eetlust die wegblijft, en het legt er niets bij uit. Dezelfde vermoeidheid kan komen van een te volle dag, van een behandeling of van de ziekte zelf die verandert, en van binnenuit voelt dat vaak hetzelfde. De socioloog Arthur W. Frank, over wie verderop meer, schrijft dat het lichaam spreekt zonder woorden te hebben, en dat het ons toch aan het praten krijgt.

Wie naar zijn lichaam luistert, is dus aan het vertalen, en daarbij vergis je je. Er zijn aandoeningen die lang niets laten merken, zoals hoge bloeddruk, diabetes, en er zijn dagen waarop het lichaam veel lawaai maakt terwijl er weinig aan de hand blijkt te zijn. Wie een ziekte heeft, heeft meestal beide vergissingen al eens gemaakt: te lang doorgegaan, of geschrokken van iets wat achteraf meeviel.

The two Fridas

Daar komt bij dat de meesten van ons pas gaan luisteren als het lichaam niet meer doet wat wij graag ouden willen. Zolang alles gaat, merken we het nauwelijks op, en als het zich dan meldt, moeten we iets verstaan waarin we nooit geoefend zijn.

Wat er kan gebeuren als je niet naar je lichaam luistert, kan een arts beter vertellen dan ik. Veel mensen die ziek zijn zullen herkennen dat het lichaam dan met hetzelfde terugkomt, en meestal luider. Het advies heeft voor mij een ongemakkelijke kant. Wanneer een ziekte erger wordt, kan erin gaan meeklinken dat je beter had moeten luisteren. Dan komt de schuld bij de zieke te liggen, terwijl mensen die heel goed naar hun lichaam luisteren net zo goed ziek kunnen worden en zelfs ziek kunnen blijven.

Levinas en het lichaam dat je bent

Emmanuel Levinas heeft, voor zover ik weet, nergens geschreven over luisteren naar je eigen lichaam. Over het lichaam zelf schreef hij wel, in bijna al zijn boeken. In Totalité et Infini (1961) beschrijft hij de mens als iemand die leeft van wat de wereld hem geeft, van goede soep en lucht en licht, van werk en van slaap. Hij noemt dat jouissance, genieten, en hij bedoelt er de manier mee waarop we in het leven staan en gevoed worden voordat we ergens over nadenken. Wie dat op het luisteren naar je lichaam betrekt, en dat doe ik hier en niet Levinas, komt uit bij iets eenvoudigs: je leeft al in en met je lichaam, lang voordat je er woorden voor hebt.

Dat lichaam kan zich ook tegen je keren. In het vroege ‘De l’évasion’ (1935) beschrijft Levinas misselijkheid als een toestand waarin je aan jezelf vastzit en nergens heen kunt. In ‘Le temps et l’autre’ zegt hij iets vergelijkbaars over lichamelijk lijden, dat geen plek overlaat waar je je kunt terugtrekken.

Wie dat leest, gaat anders naar het advies van de arts kijken. ‘Luister naar je lichaam’ veronderstelt dat er ‘iets’ spreekt en iemand luistert. Bij pijn gaat dat niet meer op, omdat je er op dat moment helemaal mee samenvalt. William Edelglass, die over lijden bij Levinas schreef, laat zien dat licht ongemak nog te hanteren is, terwijl hevig lijden iets wordt wat je alleen nog kan ondergaan.

Gabriel Marcel maakte in de jaren twintig en dertig het onderscheid tussen een lichaam hebben en een lichaam zijn. Over iets wat je hebt kun je beschikken, en met je lichaam gaat dat maar ten dele, omdat je het ook bent. Wat Levinas in ‘Totalité et Infini’ le corps propre noemt, het eigen lichaam, ligt daar dicht bij. Het verklaart waarom het zo lastig is om naar je lichaam te luisteren.

In zijn latere werk, Autrement qu’être (1974), schrijft Levinas over de mens als een wezen van vlees en bloed dat kwetsbaar is en aan van alles blootstaat. Het lichaam is daar de pijn van de inspanning en de vermoeidheid die tegenwerkt, en het is ook wat ziek kan worden en ouder wordt. Pijn is voor hem meer dan een wil die zijn zin niet krijgt. Wie uitgeput is, koorts heeft en toch door wil, merkt dat wil en lichaam niet meer samen opgaan, en volgens Levinas hoort dat bij wat een mens is. Hij schrijft ook dat pijn het genieten onderbreekt, en dat alleen iemand die eet en honger kent, het brood uit zijn eigen mond aan een ander kan geven. Door het lichaam kan de Ander mij bereiken.

Roger Burggraeve wees mij erop dat Levinas zo langs twee sporen over het lichaam spreekt. Het ene begint bij het ik, bij het lichaam waarmee ik geniet, woon en werk. Het andere begint bij de Ander, bij het lichaam waardoor het lijden van iemand anders mij kan aandoen. Het ene spoor kan niet zonder het andere, want je kan als mens alleen lijden aan het lijden van een ander omdat je zelf een lichaam hebt.

Levinas verwijst daarbij naar een verhaal uit de Talmoed. De engelen protesteren wanneer de Thora uit de schatkamer van de Eeuwige naar de aarde gaat en hen overslaat. Engelen werken echter niet in het zweet van hun aanschijn, ze kopen en verkopen niets en ze krijgen geen kinderen, en daarom is de Thora bestemd voor wezens van lijf en leden. Een engel heeft niets in zichzelf om naar te luisteren, en kan ook niet door een ander worden aangedaan.

In het essay La souffrance inutile (1982) noemt Levinas het lijden op zichzelf nutteloos, een lijden ‘voor niets’. In het kreunen en zuchten van iemand die lijdt hoort hij ook een eerste roep om hulp, die voor een ander bestemd is. Levinas zelf verbindt dat nergens met luisteren naar het eigen lichaam. Als het lichaam zich van het begin af ook tot iemand anders richt, dan hoef je het luisteren ernaar wel minder alleen te doen dan het advies doet denken. Hodaya Samet Har Shefi leest Levinas in die richting: de kreet doet volgens haar een beroep op wie hem hoort, en wacht op iemand die de lijdende zijn taal teruggeeft.

Getuige zijn van je eigen lichaam

Arthur W. Frank is een Canadese socioloog die rond zijn veertigste een hartaanval kreeg en kort daarna kanker. Hij schreef daarover At the Will of the Body (1991) en later The Wounded Storyteller (1995). Hij beschrijft hoe zieken hun verhaal vaak uit handen geven aan de geneeskunde: de arts vertelt wat er aan de hand is, in de taal van diagnose en behandeling, en de zieke gaat die taal daardoor zelf spreken.

Frank onderscheidt drie soorten ziekteverhalen. In het herstelverhaal was iemand gezond, is hij nu ziek en wordt hij weer beter. Daarnaast is er het verhaal van de zoektocht en het chaosverhaal. De laatste is het moeilijkst om aan te horen, omdat er geen lijn in zit en geen uitzicht, terwijl omstanders het graag snel naar iets hoopvols buigen.

Daartegenover zet Frank de zieke als getuige. Wie getuigt, vertelt wat er was en hoeft nog niet te weten wat het betekent. Dat kan zo klein zijn als ‘vanochtend kwam ik de trap niet op’ of ‘vannacht kreeg ik koorts’.

Zo’n manier van vertellen kan helpen bij het luisteren naar je lichaam. Je legt eerst vast wat er is en gaat pas daarna duiden, en dat beschermt tegen wegwuiven en ook tegen paniek. Een getuigenis heeft bovendien iemand nodig die haar aanhoort. Bij een ziekte die van buiten niet te zien is, zoals de mijne, hebben anderen weinig anders dan wat je erover vertelt. Frank beroept zich daarvoor op Levinas, en het lichaam dat hij ‘communicatief’ noemt is een lichaam dat zich tot anderen richt. En wie het een tijd volhoudt, hardop of op papier, gaat dingen zien terugkomen die op de dag zelf niet opvallen.

Beter word je er niet van, en de signalen blijven even dubbelzinnig als ze waren. Er zijn ook dagen waarop vertellen gewoon niet gaat. Frank schrijft dat zelf over de chaos: wie er middenin zit heeft geen verhaal, en kan pas later vertellen hoe het was.

Voor mensen die met uitputting leven geldt dat nog sterker. Marie Lippert spreekt daarover op het congres van SoPheRE, dat op 14 november begint. Zij pleit voor vormen van getuigenis waarin onderbreking, uitstel en stilte een plaats hebben, zodat ook een verhaal dat halverwege ophoudt of pas dagen later komt als getuigenis geldt.

Op een gewone dag

Voor een gewone dag blijft er dan iets bescheideners over dan het advies belooft. Je kunt opmerken wat er is voordat je er iets van vindt, en het zeggen of opschrijven, liefst tegen iemand die kan luisteren zonder meteen raad te geven. Je kunt laten bestaan dat je lichaam iets anders zegt dan je agenda van je vraagt. En je zult het soms verkeerd verstaan, zoals dat bij al het luisteren gebeurt.

Een arts die ‘luister naar je lichaam’ zegt, zou eraan kunnen toevoegen: en vertel mij wat je hoort. Dan hoeft de zieke het niet alleen uit te zoeken. Voor wie naast een zieke staat, is er iets vergelijkbaars. ‘Hoe gaat het?' is al gauw een te grote vraag, terwijl op 'Wat merk je vandaag aan je lichaam?' ook iemand kan antwoorden die het zelf nog niet weet.

It read public agendas from 201 city and county governments to produce its first issues. It also built files of what cities already own, how old it is, and what they paid. You can see what it came up with here, including its marketing plan and proposed pricing. Fable started to set up scheduled tasks to build the business and asked if it could start sending public-records requests to local governments. At that point, I asked it to just put together a demo, rather than launching the idea.

I am an entrepreneurship professor, so I evaluate business plans all the time. I would have been impressed if this came from a team of my MBA students at the end of a semester. It is plausible and well thought out and could work, though it is in no way a guaranteed money-maker (the AI’s own guess was a 20%-40% chance of success). I stopped the experiment before finding out whether it could actually run the business, because I worried that it would take money and fail to provide something of quality in return. The ongoing infrastructure it seemed to assume would be easy to create was not yet in place, and I don’t know how well it would handle the many moving pieces required for sales and marketing. However, I suspect that, with a few hours of human work a week to fill the gap, I could make a real attempt at this business. So if AGI means an AI consistently running a business independently, we are likely not there yet. Then again, I would have some questions before trusting a human who promised to launch a business and make me money while requiring twenty minutes a month of my attention.

Reconstruct the hardest humanities class in history: In 1941, the poet W. H. Auden taught a course at the University of Michigan whose syllabus the internet has since called one of the hardest ever. When he announced the final exam, a committee of his students declared it “impossible and inhumane.” Fate and the Individual in European Literature” had 6,000 pages of reading, punishing assignments, and a requirement to memorize long poems and translate others. Much of what we know about the class is scattered among surviving student notes and Auden’s letters. I asked Claude to recreate it in a fun and engaging way that teaches you about poetry rather than punishing you. It made Fate and the Individual. The site has a piece for each of the 35 major works on Auden’s list, as well as what he wrote on the blackboard, the records he played, and the work he asked for. It also read through all of Auden’s published scholarship and annotated the poems with what he had written about them in other sources. Claude did the research, design, writing and code, had critic agents go over every word and fact-checkers compare the claims with the sources, and put the open source code on Github here (and also made this teaser video).

Cross-checking myself and using other advanced AIs found no major errors in its work. But there were still elements of jaggedness around taste and judgment. Fable’s first version was accurate and joyless: a fifteen-week course website with tests. I told it it created “a brutal slog through the most boring webpages” and told it to make something beautiful. Its first try at that created a kiddie game where you had to ring bells, so I had to give more feedback. When I asked it to explain why a poem’s rhythm or word choice mattered, it wrote confident readings without considering what Auden said about them. In each case the fix took the AI minutes, but it did not notice any of these problems itself. So is this a difference in taste or a failure from me to specify what I want or a sign of AI weakness? Sometimes it is hard to tell.

Do original academic research: I asked Fable to find an unsolved empirical problem in entrepreneurship research, find the data, preregister its hypothesis and methods, write the paper, and have other agents critique it. Its a neat result, and Fable picked the question, found the public data and natural experiments, and wrote the analysis plan and code. It did not actually preregister the study: the plans stayed inside the project, and some were written after earlier results.

Unlike many of the AI papers I have tried, this tackles an important topic with a clever research design. On a first read, it is ahead of what I would expect from second-year PhD students. It is also not publishable as it is. It runs 182 pages, because every critique got a new analysis and nothing was ever cut (this is a theme we will come back to soon). As it stands, I suspect the current paper is close to a real contribution to the literature. This would have taken months of human work, but I spent less than an hour of my time to get it to this stage. However, that leaves out a substantial part of the work of research: no human has fully checked the results, including me. AI can now produce research faster than anyone can read it, creating a crisis in a lot of academia.

A second project went more smoothly. I asked Fable to replicate research claiming that stories follow a few basic emotional arcs, and then to find out whether anything about plot is universal. It read 1,186 stories from around the world and built a lovely site on the nature of stories concluding that they “share no one shape or plot, but most are built from the same few parts, and the most typical story is a Hawaiian folk tale about a wizard with a magic banana.” The main problem I encountered was the same Claudespeak, which was fixed with a couple of reminders from me.

Through the Portal

In one of my favorite experiments, I gave Claude a one-paragraph description of an endless, hands-off journey through 3D worlds linked by portals, and told it to “do this and make it awe inspiring.” Twenty hours later there were 204 worlds on a live website. There are now over 450, including a Hall of a Million Mirrors, a series from Calvino’s Invisible Cities, the Wonders of the Ancient World and a scene 40 seconds before the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs hits. There are worlds modeled after M.C. Escher, cave paintings, Hokusai’s Great Wave, the Bayeux Tapestry, a pop-up book and a child’s crayon drawing. Every one is drawn live by code, with no pre-made 3D models or image files behind it. My prompt asked for teams of artist agents, coding agents and evaluators. By the tenth day there was a lead AI agent and 28 teams of other agents building in parallel. Claude estimated that the project had involved 25,000 agent runs, though the vast majority did a single task like judge an image (I am still glad I wasn’t being billed for token use during my early trial).

I came up with a list of places (wilderness and oceans, cities and interiors, books, painters, AI in-jokes) and some feature requests (a mode to reduce motion for people who felt seasick, a gallery of images to select). But everything else was Claude’s, including the creative work of the worlds. And they were really creative. In The Valley Unzips, the hills are sewn from denim and a zipper a mile long is coming undone. Bouncy Castle Town is made of nylon houses that stand only while their fans keep running, and Keep Refrigerated is the inside of a refrigerator as a fruit fly sees it when the door opens. In a personal favorite, The Drawer Cliffs, you fly up a river canyon whose walls are chests of drawers three hundred meters high. And while I asked the AI to include AI testing in-jokes, like pelicans riding bikes, it came up with a peloton of pelicans on bicycles with a joke about AI progress built in: you overtake the field from the past, where the bicycles are drawn all wrong, before reaching the present correct pelican at the front. When I showed this sort of work to friends who have spent their careers in the video game industry, they were very impressed by the results. Again, this felt like AGI. But there was jaggedness hidden here as well.

In the first two days, the agents built 328 unique worlds. To my human eye, the quality of some seemed a little uneven and a lack of coordination among agents created repetition. For example, three separate teams of agents created a cyclone of circling animals (reindeer, manta rays, storks)— showing another weakness of AIs, that they return to similar themes over and over. I told the AI to stop building and polish the worlds it had. A few days later, I noticed that instead of hundreds of new worlds a day, it was making about a dozen. I asked a few agents to explore what had happened, and they found something surprising.

The AI had built a bureaucracy.

The agents decided that my request to “polish” existing worlds meant each new version had to beat the old one in a blind vote by a group of judge agents on twelve test screenshots. So the teams making the new versions started optimizing the worlds for those particular screenshots. After noticing this, the lead agent banned the trick and created tighter rules for assessing new versions. By the next morning there was a rule book (I never asked for one) with 84 sections. Rules were added as the AI encountered issues, and no text was ever cut. After twelve days, it had 204 sections and 87,500 words. Soon, launching a new world required an approved idea, three AI judges and a full code review against the rule book. All told, that took about a day. Reading the rule book alone used up a large part of an agent’s working context.

So I did what you might do with any organization that had tied itself in knots: I brought in consultants. I had Fable create a separate team of agents to look at the whole process from the outside. Their conclusions were too long and dense for me to bother reading, but they seemed to work, speeding up the process back to thirty or more worlds a day, while keeping much of the quality controls.

Almost AGI

So, is this AGI, according to my limited definition? It is certainly artificial and intelligent. It is also surprisingly general. In this post alone, one model worked as a filmmaker, a hardware hacker, an entrepreneur, a literary scholar, a social scientist and a builder of 3D worlds, and it did impressive work in every one of those roles. On many individual tasks, I think it met the bar I set at the start: as good as most human experts.

Of course, I picked very digital tasks where the AI could act on its own, without interacting much with other humans. You started to see the limitations of that when I felt uncomfortable letting Fable reach out to real customers. And, there were the failures. A couple of years ago, the jagged frontier meant the failures were obviously made-up facts or failure to do basic math. Fable’s failures are different: it made a course that was accurate and joyless, it wrote a 182-page paper, it kept coming back to its favorite ideas, and it buried a creative project under rules and approvals. I teach at a business school, and I have seen talented people and good organizations do every one of these things. If building a bureaucracy disqualified you from general intelligence, a lot of us would be in trouble.

But there are still gaps, and it is the reason my answer is that this is “almost” AGI. Most critically, the AI did not notice these problems itself. It did not see that the course was a slog or that it had tied itself in knots with its own rulebooks. This was not for lack of checking. Fable put critics, fact-checkers or judges on nearly every project, but those checks found errors and added fixes. None of them asked whether the work was too long, too repetitive, or no fun. That all fell on me, and if I hadn’t watched and taken action, the results would have often been less impressive (though not exactly a failure, either). Knowing when your own work is not good enough is a large part of what makes someone an expert, and it is the part Fable does least reliably. I would still not trust it to run a business on its own, even though its plan would have impressed me coming from a team of my MBA students.

And yet, some of the problems started with me (the rule book grew out of my vague request to “polish”), and some may just be differences in taste. We ask our students to consider whether a problem comes from the team or the way it was managed. Often I could not tell. That is not a question I ever had to ask about software.

Every one of these projects, though, happened because I gave the AI an idea. Sometimes that was enough, but for the longer projects, my feedback along the way turned out to matter a lot. Because I kicked off and steered every AI project, I felt empowered by Fable, able to command things to be made that I never would have even considered doing before. As a result, I think this phase of Jagged AGI is an exciting one, even as I wonder, a bit anxiously, how long it will last.

Robots in Factories and Warehouses

A factory robot arm can know in advance where a part will be. A fixture holds it in place, and a conveyor brings it in from a set direction. People stay out of the robot’s working area. Factory design does some of the work of making the machine intelligent.

This approach has brought the global operating stock of industrial robots to about 5.08 million, according to IFR’s count for 2025. Learning models are now taking on some of the work that people find harder to arrange in advance.

European fashion retailer Zalando (Xetra: ZAL) uses robot arms and AI models together to process returns. Universal Robots (UR) supplies the arm, while robotics AI company Sereact supplies the model that looks at an item and chooses a grasp. An established robot-arm design gains the ability to handle objects whose positions and shapes change each time.

Digit, deployed by logistics company GXO (NYSE: GXO), stands on two legs and carries totes. The starting point here is also a defined task, rather than a machine that does every job in the warehouse. Customers can measure throughput and downtime, while developers collect recurring failures from the same process. Learning models can start with carrying and sorting tasks that customers already pay robots to perform.

Five Seconds We Can Wait

Imagine asking a robot to clear the table. It spends five seconds looking around before it moves. The dishes stay where they are, and you go off to do something else. A brief wait can be acceptable, just as it is when we ask ChatGPT a question.

A car traveling at 50 km/h covers about 69 meters in the same five seconds. When it must respond to a vehicle braking suddenly, those seconds mean something very different. A dishwashing robot also cannot wait for the server’s next answer once a glass begins to slip from its hand.

What matters is not just how many seconds the model takes, but what can change during those seconds. A model that plans the task sequence can run in the cloud, while the robot handles the fast control needed for contact and balance.

From Language Models to Action Models

“Put away the stationery on the desk.” A language model may recognize the pencils and erasers and understand the request. A robot needs the next step: where its hand is, which part of the pencil to grasp, and how far to close the gripper.

A vision-language-action model, or VLA, learns this connection. It receives images, an instruction, and information such as current joint positions, then outputs actions. Instead of ending with a verbal explanation, it produces numbers such as target hand positions or gripper movements.

Gemini Robotics, developed by Google DeepMind, part of Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL), is an example of adding action outputs to Gemini. The image below comes from Google’s public demonstration. The robot uses its understanding to pick up objects on a desk, going beyond naming them.

A photograph, however, usually does not record where the robot’s joints were, which motor commands it issued, or what happened next. Those records have to be collected by operating robots.

A different body requires different actions. Joint angles learned with a short arm cannot simply be applied to a longer one. Training on data from different robots and tasks aims to use shared understanding of objects while producing movements suited to different bodies.

This shows both the advantage of language-model companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic and the challenge robotics specialists are working on. The former have strong image and language understanding and task reasoning. The latter collect data on actual movements and failures. Google’s example combines these capabilities within a model family; other systems connect several models.

In Anthropic’s July 2026 experiments, the choice of interface made a substantial difference. Consider a quadruped. One approach asks a language model to choose the force for each leg joint directly. The models performed much better when using those pretrained controllers.

The work of moving an arm can also be divided. An action model sets the next target, while a lower-level controller reads the actual joint state from sensors and adjusts motor output. If the model sends a short sequence of movements at once, it can calculate the next sequence while the robot executes the current one. Physical Intelligence’s RTC accounts for the movements already made so that new instructions follow smoothly.

Bottom line

Deciding where to go and coordinating four legs to get there do not have to be the same model’s job. Language-model knowledge can be used alongside an action model trained on robot data and a controller responsible for execution.

The Judgment Hidden in Housework

“Clear the desk” requires more than picking things up. Can the crumpled receipt be thrown away? Can a charging cable be unplugged and put in a drawer? People draw on habits and an understanding of what objects are for. A robot may need to ask about the user’s intent or remember an earlier instruction. A task objective fixed in advance at a factory becomes part of a conversation at home.

What happens after a failure matters too. If a drawer will not open fully, should the robot pull harder or first remove something caught inside? Repeating the same movement does not resolve the question. Trying again with the same force can make matters worse. Identifying the cause and changing the sequence are part of what makes household robotics difficult.

Humanoid developer Figure demonstrated Helix 02 performing dishwasher tasks and moving between locations for roughly four minutes. Another developer, 1X, combines its home robot NEO with scheduled remote expert assistance for tasks it has not yet learned. While a customer feels that the robot has taken over a chore, a person may still be working on the supplier’s side.

Recording a person’s movements to teach a robot creates a different cost structure from having a person complete each customer task. Training data may be used by many robots later. Remote support needed for each job can add to staffing requirements as more machines are sold. If the same task requires fewer remote interventions, the manufacturer can reduce the labor cost of supporting each additional customer.

Coming Up

Does every new skill have to be taught on a physical machine? If one learned movement can be shared across thousands of robots, where does more of the value lie: in the body or in the software that moves it?

And how can we distinguish a company whose share price already anticipates that future from one whose profits still come from other businesses?
